description: A comprehensive study of the behavior of electrical circuits, network theorems, transient responses, and AC/DC analysis in Electrical Engineering.

sections.title: Kirchhoff's Laws and Basic Concepts
sections.description: Fundamental laws for solving the distribution of voltage and current in electrical circuits.

key_concepts.explanation: Based on the conservation of charge. The algebraic sum of currents entering and leaving any node or junction in a circuit is exactly zero.
Based on the conservation of energy. The algebraic sum of all voltage drops and electromotive forces (EMFs) in any closed loop or mesh is zero.

equations: Delta to Star: R1 = (Rb * Rc) / (Ra + Rb + Rc)
Star to Delta: Ra = (R1 * R2 + R2 * R3 + R3 * R1) / R1

sections.title: Network Theorems
sections.description: Powerful analytical techniques for simplifying complex linear circuits into equivalent, manageable models.

steps.title: Finding Thevenin Equivalent Circuit
steps.detail: First, remove the load resistance from the circuit. Then, calculate the open-circuit voltage across those terminals to find the Thevenin Voltage (Vth).

steps.title: Calculating Thevenin Resistance (Rth)
steps.detail: Deactivate all independent sources (short-circuit voltage sources and open-circuit current sources) and calculate the equivalent resistance looking back into the load terminals.

cases.condition: Maximum Power Transfer Theorem is applied
results: Maximum power is transferred from source to load when the load resistance (RL) equals the Thevenin equivalent resistance (Rth) of the network. (RL = Rth)
The value of maximum power transferred is Pmax = (Vth^2) / (4 * Rth)
Valid only for linear and bilateral networks containing more than one independent source.
Cannot be used for power calculations because power is a non-linear function (depends on the square of voltage or current).

sections.title: Transient Analysis
sections.description: The study of the time-dependent behavior of currents and voltages in RL, RC, and RLC circuits during switching operations.

formulas.category: Time Constants and General Transient Equation
equations: Time constant of RC circuit: tau = R * C
Time constant of RL circuit: tau = L / R
General Equation: x(t) = x(final) + [x(initial) - x(final)] * e^(-t/tau)

key_concepts.explanation: Immediately after a switching action, an uncharged capacitor acts as a short circuit because it opposes sudden changes in voltage. An unenergized inductor acts as an open circuit because it opposes sudden changes in current.

sections.title: AC Analysis and Resonance
sections.description: Analysis of alternating current circuits, focusing on impedance, phasors, and the phenomenon of resonance.

results: Total circuit impedance (Z) is at its absolute minimum and equals the resistance (R).
The current flowing through the circuit reaches its maximum value.
The circuit operates at a unity power factor (pf = 1).
Total circuit impedance (Z) is at its maximum value (Dynamic Impedance Z = L / (C * R)).
The main line current drawn from the supply is at its minimum.
The circuit operates at a unity power factor.

sections.title: Two-Port Networks
sections.description: Mathematical modeling of networks using parameters that relate the input port voltages and currents to the output port voltages and currents.

key_concepts.explanation: Currents I1 and I2 are considered the independent variables. A network is symmetrical if Z11 = Z22 and reciprocal if Z12 = Z21.
Voltages V1 and V2 are considered the independent variables. These parameters are particularly useful for analyzing parallel connected two-port networks.

key_concepts.notation_or_symbol: V1 = A*V2 - B*I2 ; I1 = C*V2 - D*I2
key_concepts.explanation: These parameters relate the input variables (V1, I1) directly to the output variables (V2, -I2). They are extensively used in analyzing cascaded networks and power transmission lines.
